name: Phenol-croton oil peel

lead: A phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for wrinkles and skin tightening. The classic 1962 Baker-Gordon formula has largely been replaced by lower-concentration versions.
Evidence is mostly surgeon case series, formula studies and lab work rather than randomized trials.

paras: Croton oil is reported to be the main active peeling agent, with phenol acting as a carrier at lower concentrations; the peel injures the skin deeply and is followed by collagen remodeling.
Deeper peels carry more complications: prolonged redness, pigment change, atrophy and scarring. They are performed by physicians, often with sedation.

lead: The phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for facial resurfacing, wrinkle reduction and skin tightening. The classic Baker-Gordon formula, published in 1962, was long considered the standard for deep facial resurfacing.[1][2]

Reviews report that classical high-phenol formulas have largely been replaced by formulas with lower phenol and croton oil concentrations, which are described as having a better safety profile and more natural results, without the complete pigment loss once typical of deep peels.[1] Research by plastic surgeon Gregory Hetter argued that croton oil, rather than phenol, is the peel's active ingredient.[2][3]

paras: Phenol-croton oil peels are applied by a physician and cause a controlled deep injury to the skin. Wikipedia notes that early versions were very painful and often used general anesthesia, whereas newer formulations can be used under sedation.[4] Modified formulas use phenol as a carrier at concentrations between 16% and 50% with croton oil providing the peeling action.[5]

A series of 2000 papers in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery dissected the classic formula and tested variations in phenol and croton oil concentration, reporting that phenol alone below 50% had no significant peeling effect without taping and that croton oil drove peeling depth.[2][5] The series also discussed the role of plastic surgeons and of non-physician practitioners who developed their own croton oil formulas.[6][7]

A retrospective review of 47 patients who had a facelift combined with a perioral phenol-croton oil peel assessed outcomes using a validated patient satisfaction questionnaire and other objective measures, and reported central face skin tightening and wrinkle reduction.[8] A 2022 laboratory study reported that the peel increased type 1 and type 3 collagen amounts through SIRT-6 and SIRT-7 stimulation.[9] An animal model for the peel has also been described.[10] A small registered trial (NCT02848209) compared the histology of different peeling agents in undermined skin.[11]

Phenol, croton oil and other agents were used on skin by Ferdinand von Hebra in the second half of the 19th century, and phenol-croton oil peels were used covertly by early Hollywood stars before entering mainstream practice in the 1960s.[4] Baker published his simple formula in 1962.[2]

Deep peels carry more complications than lighter peels, with reported risks including prolonged redness, pigmentary change, atrophy, textural change and scarring.[4] The 2019 JAAD review describes the improved safety of lower-concentration formulas.[1]

timeline.event: Baker publishes the classic phenol-croton oil formula.[2]
Hetter publishes a series dissecting the formula.[2][5]
JAAD review describes modern lower-concentration deep peels.[1]
